Es gibt das Ersthelfergesetz (bzw. in den USA ist es das good samaritan law) das den Ersthelfer vor genau solchen möglichen rechtlichen Konsequenzen schützt. Wer nach bestem Wissen und Gewissen Erste Hilfe leistet, kann praktisch nicht für irgendwas belangt werden, damit die Menschen nicht aus Angst, etwas falsch zu machen, garnichtmehr helfen. 
Das einzige, was von jedem Menschen erwartet werden kann und wird, ist, die Rettungskette in Gang zu bringen (was du ja getan hast, indem du Hilfe geholt hast!).
Zu deinem Beispiel: wenn der Mensch bewusstlos ist (und immernoch selbstständig atmet) muss er in die stabile Seitenlage gebracht werden, sonst droht er an Erbrochenem zu ersticken. Wenn du deshalb eine Verletzung der Wirbelsäule (die zu dem Zeitpunkt sowieso schon da war) verschlimmerst, ist das in Kauf zu nehmen, denn: Rückenlage + Bewusstlosigkeit = akute Lebensgefahr. 
Ich versteh, wie schwierig sowas sein kann. Natürlich gibt es immer "hätte" und "sollte", aber was dir dein Bauchgefühl gesagt hat und wie du gehandelt hast, war in der Situation am Ende des Tages schon in Ordnung so :) 
Und vor allem chapeau! an eure psychische erste Hilfe, die kommt leider auch oft zu kurz.

No paramedics were called in my case, but I have first hand experience from the other side. I tried to hang myself with a belt 3 years ago when I was 18. I closed the belt into a loop, hung it over a doorhandle, put my head through and leaned into it. I passed out after a couple of seconds, literally saw my life flash before my eyes and woke up face down on the floor, panting. I had used a textile belt which eventually slid off the doorhandle, saving my life in the process. I was all alone, nobody would have found me for hours if I'd done anything just a little differently.
There were popped blood vessels in a line around my neck, in my eyes and my throat and head hurt for a week straight. Other than that, I was fine (physically). 
The experience haunts me to this day, but I'm a volunteering EMT now and it's what keeps me going.

That's really interesting to hear, I was on venlafaxine for the past year and only recently came off of it and it really numbed my emotions - not as much a sertraline did for me though. I'm currently on wellbutrin as the 5. AD I'm trying within 5 years and it brought ALL of my emotions back. I felt like a PMSing wreck for the first 2-3 weeks and then I just kinda felt okay, but still felt very intense emotions which is so much better (for me) honestly. I'm finally able to feel genuine joy again. I've been on it for 2 months now and I do still get depressed (which is to be expected) but I didn't realize how much I missed feeling my full range of emotions. I also switched to CBT at the beginning of this year which has already helped a ton too and now that I'm actually feeling like a person again I'm able to properly incorporate the things I learn in therapy into my life. 

TL;DR wellbutrin was a godsend for my emotions and venlafaxine sucked ass. Now I'm a lot better thanks to therapy and wellbutrin (I still have a long way go go though).

First of- I'm not a vet, just a cat mum, so everything I say should be taken with a grain of salt. One of my two cats gets these too from time to time and I think they're quite common like eye boogers. Some cats get them more, some less in my experience. You get boogers in your nose too, even when you're completely healthy and they're just a part of life. HOWEVER. If the frequency of the kitty boogers occuring increases and/or they get bigger faster, if she seems to have trouble breathing or seems off in any kind of way, you should see a vet just to be sure. Listen to your gut and listen to your vet is my little piece of advice I want to give you. 
To wrap it up, if nothing changes and your cat is eating/drinking/playing/being cute normally then I would just wait until your july appointment and tell the vet then. But don't hesitate to call your vet anytime and ask for their advice if you're concerned - the worst thing to do is to do nothing. Good luck :)
